concept.name: Position trading
concept.definition: A trading style in which positions are held for weeks to months (or longer) to capture major price trends, with decisions driven mainly by macro trends, fundamentals, or long-horizon technical analysis. The term is sometimes used interchangeably with buy and hold, though position traders may actively exit when the underlying thesis or long-term trend ends.
concept.intuition: Position traders ignore daily noise and try to own an asset for the big part of a long move, reviewing the thesis periodically rather than watching the tape.
concept.mechanics: Entries are based on long-term trend signals (e.g., weekly charts, macro or fundamental theses); stops are wide and positions are reviewed weekly or monthly rather than intraday. Transaction costs are low because turnover is low, but capital is exposed to drawdowns over long holding periods.
concept.failure_modes: Wide stops mean large per-trade losses when a long-term thesis is wrong; secular reversals or value traps can hold capital in losing positions for years.
concept.misconceptions: That position trading is identical to passive buy-and-hold indexing; position traders actively select securities and exit when trends or theses fail, whereas buy and hold implies no market timing at all.
concept.example: A trader goes long an equity index ETF after a weekly golden cross, holds for nine months through interim corrections, and exits when the weekly trend breaks.
